To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the mere proximity between replication-blocking lesions leads to a strong inhibition of HR, which in turn increases the use of the mutagenic TLS.
the proximity of replication-blocking DNA lesions in the genome leads to the inhibition of homologous recombined-based lesion bypass and to an increase in error-prone trans-lesion DNA synthesis.
the proximity of replication-blocking DNA lesions leads to a strong local inhibition of HR, which increases the use of error-prone TLS and mutagenesis in the cell.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the mechanisms used by the cell to tolerate DNA lesions.
the mechanisms that control DNA repair and tolerance to DNA damage.

the mechanisms of DNA damage tolerance in Escherichio coli, which is a model system to study DNA metabolism in bacteria, and is relevant to understand the mechanisms of DNA metabolism in other organisms, including humans.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the balance between TLS and HR is modulated by the proximity of the lesions and this is independent of the activation of the SOS response.
the proximity between DNA lesions in a cell is a major determinant of the mutagenesis during a genotoxic challenge, and that it is a major factor that defines the balance between TLS and HR.
the mere proximity between two replication-blocking lesions is sufficient to trigger the activation of TLS, which is the main pathway for lesion tolerance during SOS induction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cell’s response to genotoxic stress is highly influenced by the distribution of lesions in the genome.
the cell has a way of detecting the proximity of DNA lesions and that this information is used to modulate the balance between TLS and HR.
the proximity of DNA lesions in the genome of E. coli is a key factor in determining the balance between error-free HR and error-prone TLS during lesion bypass.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the spatial arrangement of lesions in a cell’s genome is critical in determining how the cell will respond to a genotoxic stress, and that the proximity of lesions is a major determinant of the balance between TLS and HR.
, in E. coli, the proximity of replication-blocking DNA lesions in a genome can strongly modulate the balance between error-free HR and error-prone TLS pathways during lesion bypass.
the proximity of lesions can modulate the choice of DNA repair pathways, and that the balance between TLS and HR can be modulated by local changes in DNA structure.
